articles.title_original: Two-dimensional turbulent condensates without bottom drag
articles.title_en: Two-Dimensional Turbulent Condensates Without Bottom Drag
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract The extent to which equilibrium statistical theory is applicable to driven dissipative dynamics remains an important open question in many systems. We use extensive direct numerical simulations (DNS) of the incompressible two-dimensional (2D) Navier–Stokes equation to examine the steady state of large-scale condensates in 2D turbulence at finite Reynolds number Re in the absence of bottom drag. Large-scale condensates appear above a critical Reynolds number Rec≈4.19. Close to this onset, we find a power-law scaling of the energy with Re-Rec, with the energy spectrum at large scales following the absolute equilibrium form proposed by Kraichnan. At larger Re, the energy spectrum deviates from this form, displaying a steep power-law range at low wavenumbers with exponent -5, with most of the energy dissipation occurring within the condensate at large scales. We show that this spectral exponent is consistent with the logarithmic radial vorticity profile of the condensate vortices predicted by quasi-linear theory for a viscously saturated condensate. Our findings shed new light on the classical problem of large-scale turbulent condensation in forced dissipative 2D flows in finite domains, showing that the large scales are close to equilibrium dynamics in weakly turbulent flows but not in the strong condensate regime with Re≫1. This article is part of the theme issue ‘Frontiers of turbulence and statistical physics’.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used direct numerical simulations to study large-scale condensates in forced, dissipative two-dimensional turbulence without bottom drag. They identified a critical Reynolds number for condensate formation and found a transition from near-equilibrium behavior to a steep low-wavenumber energy spectrum at higher Reynolds numbers.

articles.title_original: Fabrication and characterization of SiO₂–graphene oxide and SiO₂–graphene oxide–activated carbon composites
articles.title_en: SiO₂–Graphene Oxide Composites Show Promise for Wastewater Adsorption
articles.excerpt_original: This research presents the systematic creation and thorough analysis of binary SiO₂–graphene oxide (SiO₂–GO) and ternary SiO₂–graphene oxide–activated carbon (SiO₂–GO–AC) nanocomposites, focusing on optimized composition ratios for enhanced environmental adsorption applications. This work offers a comparative analysis of composition-specific structural development, surface shape, pore properties, and interfacial relations in binary and ternary nanocomposites, in contrast to earlier studies that concentrated on single composite structures. Through distinctive Si–O–Si, O–H, C O, and C–O functional groups, FTIR examination verified successful chemical integration, whilst XRD showed primarily amorphous formations with maintained graphene oxide and activated carbon properties. For the optimized SiO₂–GO (10:2 and 10:5) and SiO₂–GO–AC (1:2:1 and 1:1:2) compositions, FESEM showed uniform particle distribution and improved surface texture, suggesting better interfacial adaptability and accessible adsorption regions. According to BET examination, the SiO₂–GO (10:5) composite maintained a large surface area of 115.78 m² g⁻¹ with a well-formed Type IV mesoporous structure, while the SiO₂–GO (10:2) composite displayed a maximum surface area (127.03 m² g⁻¹). Although the (1:1:2) component offered improved micropore dominant for specific adsorption, the ternary SiO₂–GO–AC (1:2:1) composite showed a hierarchical micro-mesoporous network with significant adsorbate–adsorbent relationships. The optimized nanocomposites show great potential as effective adsorbents for microplastics, heavy metals, dyes, and other developing pollutants in sustainable wastewater treatment due to their better structural strength, porosity, and surface reactivity.
articles.summary_en: Researchers fabricated and characterized SiO₂–graphene oxide and SiO₂–graphene oxide–activated carbon nanocomposites with optimized porous structures and surface areas up to 127.03 m²/g. The materials demonstrated potential for removing microplastics, heavy metals, dyes, and other pollutants in wastewater treatment.

articles.title_original: Dynamic magnetic properties of Graphene/Fullerene/Graphene sandwich structure based on the Monte Carlo Method
articles.title_en: Monte Carlo Study Maps Magnetic Tunability of Graphene–Fullerene–Graphene Structures
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract The dynamic magnetic response and hysteresis characteristics of a mixed-spin Ising model constructed on the graphene/fullerene/graphene (G/F/G) sandwich architecture are systematically examined using the Monte Carlo method. By sweeping key intrinsic and extrinsic control parameters,including intra-and inter-layer exchange couplings (Ja, Jb, Jab), single-ion anisotropies (Da, Db), and the defining components of the applied magnetic field ( amplitude h0, period τ, and static bias field hb), while the rich spectrum of magnetically ordered states is uncovered. The system hosts Néel-type magnetization profiles, exhibits single and double compensation points (Tcomp1, Tcomp2), and undergoes well-defined dynamic phase transitions marked by a critical temperature (TC). Constructed phase diagrams map the sensitive dependence of TC and Tcomp on each parameter, while the dynamic hysteresis loops display pronounced reshaping, area evolution, and positional shifts driven by the interplay between intrinsic relaxation and sublattice-resolved field sensitivity. These findings quantitatively clarify the magnetic tunability of G/F/G heterostructures and offer actionable guidance for designing multi-state spintronic devices.
articles.summary_en: A theoretical Monte Carlo analysis identifies dynamic phase transitions, compensation points, and tunable hysteresis in graphene/fullerene/graphene heterostructures. The results suggest design parameters for multi-state spintronic devices, but provide no experimental validation or commercial evidence.

articles.title_original: Beyond Hexagonal Boron Nitride: First-Principles Study of Pentaoctite-BN and Pop-BN Monolayers
articles.title_en: First-Principles Study Identifies Tunable Non-Hexagonal BN Monolayers
articles.excerpt_original: We investigate two novel non-hexagonal boron nitride monolayers, pentaoctite-BN (PO-BN) and pop-BN (PP-BN), using first-principles calculations. Their structural, electronic, mechanical, vibrational, thermal, and optical properties are systematically analyzed to assess their stability and potential applications. Despite being metastable with respect to hexagonal BN, both polymorphs satisfy the criteria for dynamical, mechanical, and thermal stability, indicating that they are viable two-dimensional materials. Both systems are indirect-gap semiconductors whose electronic states near the band edges are dominated by out-of-plane pz orbitals. Their distinct pentagon-octagon ring networks also give rise to different in-plane elastic anisotropies. Many-body optical calculations reveal strong excitonic effects and pronounced polarization-dependent optical absorption, with lattice engineering shifting the optical response from the ultraviolet toward the visible and infrared regions. These findings demonstrate that engineering non-hexagonal lattice architectures provides an effective strategy for tuning the electronic and optical properties of two-dimensional BN, highlighting PO-BN and PP-BN as promising candidates for future optoelectronic and photonic applications.
articles.summary_en: Researchers theoretically evaluate pentaoctite-BN and pop-BN monolayers, finding dynamical, mechanical, and thermal stability despite metastability relative to hexagonal BN. Their anisotropic mechanics and polarization-dependent optical absorption suggest potential for tunable optoelectronic and photonic applications.

articles.title_original: Porous Ultralow‐ κ sp 2 ‐Bonded Boron Nitride Thin Films as Copper Diffusion Barriers
articles.title_en: Porous Boron Nitride Films Show Ultralow Dielectric Constant and Copper Barrier Performance
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Dielectric materials with low dielectric constant ( κ < 2) are highly needed to overcome a series of problems caused by the decreasing size of microelectronics. An effective way to reduce dielectric constant is introducing void structure in dielectric materials, however challenging in mechanical strength and wetting properties. Herein, porous sp 2 ‐bonded boron nitride (BN) films are directly grown on Si substrates via radio frequency magnetron sputtering. The Guinier plot analysis of grazing incidence small‐angle X‐ray scattering spectra and electron microscopy confirms the pore size of ∼1.85 nm. The porous BN (p‐BN) films show a band gap of ∼5.88 eV and a hydrophobic surface, ensuring the stability of dielectric properties. P‐BN films exhibit an ultralow‐ κ of 1.77 at 100 kHz. These porous ultralow‐ κ BN films are electrically robust and mechanically stable superior to the previously reported porous dielectrics and close to the referent dense amorphous BN and hexagonal BN. Additionally, the p‐BN films demonstrate notable diffusion barrier capability, effectively blocking Cu diffusion even with a thickness as low as 3 nm. This work provides a viable approach towards the controlled synthesis of porous ultralow‐ κ BN films as versatile dielectrics for transistor gate barriers, passivation layers, and capacitor spacers in high‐performance electronics.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed porous sp2-bonded boron nitride thin films with a dielectric constant of 1.77 and demonstrated effective copper-diffusion blocking at thicknesses as low as 3 nm. The films could serve as gate barriers, passivation layers, and capacitor spacers in advanced electronics.

articles.title_original: Monolithic 2D Synapse‐Neuron Integration via Defect‐Engineered h‐BN for Energy‐Efficient Neuromorphic Computing
articles.title_en: Defect-Engineered h-BN Enables Monolithic Synapse–Neuron Computing
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Neuromorphic computing offers a route to overcome the von Neumann bottleneck by emulating coupled synaptic and neuronal functions. However, monolithic integration of these components remains challenging due to mismatches in material platforms, operating mechanisms, and device architectures. Here, we exploit defect‐engineered hexagonal boron nitride (h‐BN) to realize a monolithic synapse–neuron platform within a unified 2D materials system. An optoelectronic synapse based on a MoS 2 /h‐BN heterostructure and a filamentary neuron formed in an Ag/h‐BN/graphite stack are spatially separated yet electrically coupled through a shared h‐BN dielectric. Under ultraviolet illumination and gate bias, defects in h‐BN and at the h‐BN/SiO 2 interface are activated, enabling tunable, reversible, and retained multilevel conductance that emulates both short‐ and long‐term plasticity. The synapse supports 8‐bit‐equivalent accessible conductance updating and 6‐bit retained state separability, enabling CIFAR‐10 inference comparable to software baselines. Volatile h‐BN filaments provide threshold switching and leaky integrate‐and‐fire dynamics. In a one‐neuron–one‐synapse configuration, gate‐tunable current compliance and intrinsic neuronal thresholding suppress redundant low‐weight synaptic signals, reducing the estimated synaptic read‐current contribution by >80% with negligible accuracy degradation. This work establishes a proof‐of‐concept shared‐h‐BN platform for physically coupled synaptic storage and neuronal activation, providing a device‐level route toward energy‐efficient neuromorphic hardware.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated a monolithic neuromorphic platform combining MoS₂/h-BN synapses with Ag/h-BN/graphite filamentary neurons. The shared h-BN architecture delivered multilevel conductance, neuronal threshold switching, and an estimated >80% reduction in synaptic read-current contribution, indicating potential for energy-efficient hardware.

articles.title_original: Nonlinear dynamics and chaotic behavior of curved self-sustaining BNNTs under combined thermal and magnetic fields
articles.title_en: Study Models Chaotic Dynamics of Curved Boron Nitride Nanotubes
articles.excerpt_original: This study examines the primary resonance and chaotic vibration behavior of a curved single-walled boron nitride nanotube (CSWBNNT) subjected to axial thermo-magnetic loading and transverse harmonic excitation on a viscoelastic foundation. The system is modeled using nonlocal Euler–Bernoulli beam theory and reduced to an ordinary differential equation via a single-mode Galerkin approximation. The method of multiple scales is applied to derive analytical expressions for the primary resonance response of a clamped–clamped CSWBNNT. Parametric effects, including nonlinear contributions of the viscoelastic medium, sinusoidal curvature amplitudes, and Young’s modulus value, are investigated with emphasis on frequency response, jumping phenomena, and instability regions. Numerical simulations using the Runge–Kutta method generate bifurcation diagrams, phase plane trajectories, and Poincaré maps to characterize periodic and chaotic dynamics. Results reveal that thermo-magnetic forces strongly influence resonance behavior, while chaotic vibrations are highly sensitive to excitation amplitude, underscoring the complex interplay between external loading and nonlinear structural parameters.
articles.summary_en: Researchers model resonance, instability, and chaotic vibrations in curved single-walled boron nitride nanotubes under combined thermal and magnetic loading. The findings show that thermo-magnetic forces and excitation amplitude strongly affect nonlinear dynamic behavior, informing future nanoscale structural design.

articles.title_original: Excitonic physics and emergent phenomena in layered transition metal dichalcogenides: progress and prospects
articles.title_en: Review Highlights Excitonic Physics and Emerging Technologies in Layered TMDs
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) are a fascinating class of layered materials, distinguished by weak interlayer van der Waals forces. Their atomically thin structure and ability to form various layered assemblies provide exceptional electronic and optical properties, positioning TMDs at the forefront of condensed matter research and next-generation technologies. The presence of strong quantum confinement and reduced dielectric screening gives rise to tightly bound excitonic quasiparticles with large binding energies, enabling their existence even at room temperature. The collective interaction of these quasiparticles with other carriers or excitations yields a rich landscape of many-body effects and emergent phenomena. In this perspective, we present a unified overview of excitonic physics and many-body interactions in layered TMDs, highlighting recent developments and open challenges. We discuss how the strong quantum confinement, spin-orbit coupling, and many-body interactions shape the electronic and optical properties of various TMDs. Finally, we discuss future opportunities for TMDs-based technologies, including superabsorption, exciton crystals, single-photon emission, coupling to ferroic and correlated degrees of freedom. This perspective connects recent advances in excitonic and many-body physics in layered TMDs, highlighting emerging opportunities for quantum, photonic, and optoelectronic technologies.
articles.summary_en: A perspective reviews excitonic and many-body phenomena in layered transition metal dichalcogenides, emphasizing quantum confinement, spin–orbit coupling and reduced dielectric screening. It identifies opportunities in quantum, photonic and optoelectronic technologies, including superabsorption, exciton crystals and single-photon emission.

articles.title_original: Probing the Potential Profile of Twisted Bilayer Graphene via Fabry-Pérot Interference
articles.title_en: Fabry–Pérot Interference Maps Potential Barriers in Twisted Bilayer Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: We use Fabry-Pérot interference to probe the internal potential profile of large-angle twisted bilayer graphene. We trace anomalous resistance oscillations in the nominally unipolar regime to a hidden cavity formed by unintentional local doping in our device. By analyzing zero-field interference patterns, we determine the location and size of this inhomogeneity. Magnetotransport measurements support the model, distinguishing local cavity modes from global resonances through their different magnetic dependence. Simulations using our extracted profile reproduce the experimental features. Our results highlight interference spectroscopy as a simple, non-invasive probe for identifying local defects and internal potential barriers in ballistic devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers use Fabry–Pérot interference and magnetotransport to identify hidden doping-induced cavities and internal potential barriers in large-angle twisted bilayer graphene. The approach offers a non-invasive method for characterizing defects in ballistic graphene devices.

articles.title_original: Graphene Materials for Sustainable Energy Applications: A Contemporary Perspective
articles.title_en: Review Assesses Graphene Materials for Sustainable Energy Applications
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Graphene has garnered significant attention as a promising material with great potential for contributing to sustainable energy initiatives, such as RE100 (100% renewable energy initiative) and CF100 (100% carbon‐free initiative). This review aims to explore the potential of graphene for advancing renewable energy applications by highlighting the recent advancements in synthesis techniques, transfer methods, and interface engineering. This study delves into the fundamental properties of graphene, provides comparative analyses with other carbonaceous materials, and evaluates their application in energy storage, conversion, and harvesting. The findings reveal that graphene possesses high thermal and electrical conductivities, superior mechanical properties, and a versatile range of potential applications. However, challenges, such as scalability of production, integration with other materials, and associated costs, limit their widespread adoption. These findings suggest that graphene has the potential to drive innovative solutions in the energy sector. However, overcoming practical and economic hurdles remains essential. Although graphene presents significant transformative prospects for sustainable energy, concerted research and development efforts are imperative to fully realizing its potential in industrial applications.
articles.summary_en: This review examines graphene synthesis, transfer, and interface engineering for energy storage, conversion, and harvesting. It highlights graphene’s conductivity and mechanical properties while identifying scalability, integration, and cost as barriers to industrial adoption.

articles.title_original: Rapid synthesis of hBN on Ni foils by pre-annealing and CVD in ultra-high vacuum
articles.title_en: Ultra-High-Vacuum CVD Enables hBN Growth on Nickel Foils
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Mono- and few-layer hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) is an indispensable constituent of heterostructure stacks and prototypical devices composed of two-dimensional (2D) materials. It is therefore necessary to continuously explore new synthesis routes for hBN and optimize the existing ones, with material quality, scalability, and post-growth manipulation set as priority. Here, we study chemical vapor deposition (CVD) synthesis of hBN on polycrystalline Ni foils in ultra-high vacuum. In our approach, first a short electron-beam annealing is employed to optimize Ni grain structure and surface roughness, yielding substrates suitable for further growth of hBN monolayers. By varying CVD synthesis conditions, various hBN island morphologies are observed, along with nickel borides concentrated on the foil’s surface and forming well-defined crystallites. Overall, the optimum hBN synthesis conditions are identified, and a successful transfer of hBN to a silicon wafer is demonstrated. Our results provide guidelines for a faster and more affordable synthesis of hBN. Also, they highlight the importance of not only the hBN-substrate but also the precursor-substrate interaction on the synthesis pathway and ultimately the quality of hBN layers.
articles.summary_en: Researchers optimized pre-annealing and CVD conditions to synthesize mono- and few-layer hexagonal boron nitride on polycrystalline nickel foils. The study identified suitable growth conditions and demonstrated transfer to silicon wafers, supporting scalable fabrication of 2D heterostructures.

articles.title_original: Simulations of p‐Channel GaN‐Based Metal‐Oxide‐Semiconductor Heterostructure Field‐Effect Transistors for Normally Off Operation
articles.title_en: Simulated p-Channel GaN MOS-HFET Enables Normally-Off CMOS Power Logic
articles.excerpt_original: An improved p‐channel metal oxide semiconductor (MOS) heterostructure field effect transistor (HFET) is proposed for a normally off operation with its counterpart n‐channel MOS‐HEMT in a CMOS GaN HFET power logic technology. The performance of the p‐channel MOS‐HFET is simulated using Silvaco device TCAD based on a transport model calibrated against experimental data. The improved MOS‐HFET design uses a combination of 2 nm AlGaN and 1 nm AlN cap layers to raise the electrostatic potential and to deplete a 2D hole gas channel below the gate contact, thereby achieving a negative threshold voltage. An increase in the drain current of more than 300% is achieved when the device is laterally scaled down to a 250 nm gate length. The proposed device exhibits a threshold voltage of approximately −4.5 V and a substantially higher on‐current of 22 mA/mm, enhancing its potential for future complementary MOS (CMOS) integrated circuits.
articles.summary_en: Simulations show that 2 nm AlGaN and 1 nm AlN cap layers can enable normally-off p-channel GaN MOS-HFET operation with an approximately −4.5 V threshold voltage. Scaling to a 250 nm gate length increased drain current by more than 300%, reaching 22 mA/mm and supporting potential complementary GaN CMOS integration.

articles.title_original: Reconfigurable Ferroelectric‐Like Two‐Dimensional Electron Gas at Room Temperature
articles.title_en: Room-Temperature Ferroelectric-Like 2DEG Enables Reconfigurable Electronics
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Engineering ferroelectric two‐dimensional electron gases (2DEGs) offers a promising route toward nonvolatile and reconfigurable electronic functionalities, yet room temperature implementations remain scarce. Here, we report a room temperature ferroelectric‐like 2DEG at the SrO‐ interface between (001) (STO) and (KNN) thin films. Robust ferroelectricity is confirmed by piezoforce microscopy, optical second harmonic generation, Nb‐/Ti‐ edges x‐ray linear dichroism, scanning transmission electron microscopy, and macroscopic polarization measurements. The ferroelectric polarization enables nonvolatile control of interfacial transport and the realization of reconfigurable conducting channels with arbitrary geometry at room temperature. The coupling between ferroelectric order and 2DEG conductivity arises from the extension of the polarization into the interfacial unit cells hosting the electron gas. These results establish / heterostructures as a ferroelectric‐like oxide electronic platform, opening pathways for low‐power, nonvolatile electronic and spin‐orbitronic devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report a room-temperature ferroelectric-like two-dimensional electron gas at the SrO interface between oxide thin films. Polarization provides nonvolatile control of interfacial transport and enables conducting channels with arbitrary geometries, potentially supporting low-power electronic and spin-orbitronic devices.

articles.title_original: Trion Excitations in Twisted Bilayer Graphene: A Quantum Monte Carlo Study
articles.title_en: Quantum Monte Carlo reveals Dirac trions in twisted bilayer graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Determining the nature of charge carriers is a fundamental goal in the study of strongly correlated electron systems. Here, we employ the continuous-field momentum-space quantum Monte Carlo method to reveal exotic "Dirac trion" excitations in the finite-temperature normal state of twisted bilayer graphene. While the ground state is a symmetry-breaking insulator with gapped ($\sim$ 20 meV) electron-like excitations, we show that a small temperature ($\sim$ 3 meV), well below the interaction scale, drives the system into a strongly fluctuating symmetric normal state. We demonstrate that this normal state hosts gapless excitations consisting of three-particle bound states, two electrons and one hole, that are exactly orthogonal to the higher-energy electrons at the zero-momentum gapless point. These Dirac trions have the remarkable property of being arbitrarily light despite being composed of heavy constituents, and their spectra can be easily tuned by varying the twist angle and interlayer hopping strength. Our unbiased quantum many-body computation sheds light on the Dirac trions in a projected correlated flat-band setting and opens the door for further investigation of many-body excitations in strongly correlated topological bands beyond Landau levels.
articles.summary_en: Researchers predict gapless three-particle bound states—two electrons and one hole—in the finite-temperature normal state of twisted bilayer graphene. The excitations are theoretically tunable through twist angle and interlayer hopping, offering insight into correlated topological bands.

articles.title_original: Anomalous metal and superconducting phases in rhombohedral graphene
articles.title_en: Rhombohedral graphene reveals tunable anomalous-metal and superconducting phases
articles.excerpt_original: Two-dimensional superconductivity is now well established in graphene-based systems, with many such realizations showing evidence for unconventional pairing. Yet in several of the gate-tuned phases that otherwise exhibit clear signatures of superconductivity, the resistance does not vanish as temperature is lowered, instead saturating at a finite value. Here we report a systematic study of this behavior in rhombohedral graphene on a WSe$_2$ substrate, finding regions of gate space with zero-resistance superconductivity alongside others with finite saturation resistance. At zero magnetic field, these regions appear as isolated pockets in gate space that otherwise exhibit strikingly similar phenomenology, including abrupt transitions to the normal state as temperature, perpendicular magnetic field, and current are raised above critical values. A small in-plane field expands and merges these pockets without qualitatively altering their behavior, producing a sharp boundary at millikelvin base temperature between states of zero or finite resistance. The finite-resistance state reproduces key phenomenology associated with the anomalous metal, a state that has been observed in thin-film superconductors for decades but lacks an accepted theoretical explanation. The tunability and reproducibility of ultra-clean rhombohedral graphene place strong constraints on extrinsic explanations and provide a new platform for understanding this behavior.
articles.summary_en: Researchers observed both zero-resistance superconductivity and finite-resistance anomalous-metal states in ultra-clean rhombohedral graphene on a WSe₂ substrate. The reproducible, gate- and field-tunable behavior offers a platform for testing explanations of anomalous metallicity and unconventional superconductivity.

articles.title_original: Sustainable mechanochemical production of amino graphene for enhanced electrothermal carbon dioxide capture
articles.title_en: Mechanochemical amino graphene improves electrothermal CO₂ capture
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Graphene-based materials are particularly attractive for electrothermal swing adsorption (ETSA)-driven CO 2 capture because of their exceptional electrical and thermal conductivities. However, the intrinsic chemical inertness of pristine graphene hinders preferential CO 2 binding from gas mixtures, yielding low adsorption capacity and poor selectivity. In addition, the scalable production of functional graphene for industrial-level CO 2 capture remains a critical challenge. Herein, polyamine-assisted mechanochemistry (PAME) is demonstrated as an impactful and scalable approach for producing ultrathin graphene nanosheet-polyethyleneimine (GNs-PEI) composites. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal strong binding interactions of 0.183 J/m 2 between graphite and polyamine, which facilitate simultaneous exfoliation and functionalization during the PAME process. The yielded GNs-PEI exhibits a high aspect ratio of 201 and an amine content of approximately 38.23 wt%. The GNs-PEI exhibited a CO 2 adsorption capacity of up to 4.77–3.44 mmol/g and a selectivity of 386 − 122 under simulated flue gas conditions (CO 2 /N 2 ratio of 15/85) at 25–55 ℃, respectively. Furthermore, GNs-PEI achieved dynamic CO 2 capacities of 3.06–3.62 mmol/g (dry) and 3.37–4.21 mmol/g (85% RH) at 25 and 50 ℃, suitable for industrial post-combustion capture. Also, the GNs-PEI demonstrated wonderful cyclic stability, retaining over 88.8% of its initial adsorption capacity after 50 temperature-swing adsorption-desorption cycles. Under a simulated ETSA process, GNs-PEI foam showed a prominent heating rate of 1.43 ℃/s at an applied bias of 8 V.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a scalable polyamine-assisted mechanochemical process to simultaneously exfoliate and functionalize graphene with polyethyleneimine. The resulting composite showed high CO₂ capacity and selectivity, humidity tolerance, cyclic stability, and rapid electrothermal heating, supporting its potential for industrial post-combustion capture.

articles.title_original: On‑Demand Design of High‑Q Metasurfaces via Physics‑Conditioned Closed‑Loop Learning
articles.title_en: Physics-Conditioned Learning Enables On-Demand Design of High-Q hBN Metasurfaces
articles.excerpt_original: Accurate modeling of spectral evolution across broad geometric parameter spaces is critical for designing high‑Q metasurfaces based on bound states in the continuum (BICs). However, conventional full‑wave simulations are too slow for practical parameter exploration, and existing deep‑learning models cannot capture both the ultra‑sharp resonances and the dynamic mode‑coupling evolution from bright resonances to hybridized states and quasi‑BICs. Here, we present a physics‑conditioned neural network (PCNN) for high‑Q metasurface design, demonstrated on hexagonal boron nitride metasurfaces that support BICs. The architecture integrates a physics‑constrained front‑end with a feature‑wise linear modulation‑conditioned U‑Net, enabling data‑efficient and high‑fidelity prediction of sharp resonances. An inverse network retrieves structural parameters from target spectra, which are validated through the forward PCNN, closing the computational design loop. We demonstrate accurate modeling and on‑demand designing of hybridized eigenstates, toroidal dipole modes, and quasi‑BICs across wide wavelength ranges (R2 > 0.96). This work provides a unified platform for studying BIC physics and realizing customizable metasurfaces for sensing, nonlinear, and topological photonics.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a physics-conditioned neural network and inverse-design workflow for modeling and designing high-Q metasurfaces based on bound states in the continuum. Demonstrated on hexagonal boron nitride metasurfaces, the approach supports customizable photonic structures for sensing, nonlinear, and topological applications while reducing reliance on slow full-wave simulations.

articles.title_original: Metal-Free Organic Photocatalysts for H2O2 Production Using Benzothiadiazole-Containing Molecules
articles.title_en: Metal-Free Organic Photocatalysts Produce Hydrogen Peroxide
articles.excerpt_original: With the growing demand of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) across various industries, there is an urgent need for a more sustainable production process to achieve a carbon-neutral economy. As an alternative to the traditional energy-intensive anthraquinone process, direct catalytic synthesis from H2 and O2 has been explored, but has significant economic, scalability, and safety concerns. Photocatalysis, which synthesizes H2O2 directly from water and oxygen using light, offers a promising solution that is greener and effectively addresses energy demands. While inorganic semiconductors have proven effective, metal-free systems are sought after to promote environmental sustainability. Organic polymeric carbon nitrides, MOFs, and COFs are being extensively studied, while porous organic cages and macrocycles, which offer better charge separation and charge transfer, have remained underexplored. This research proposes two porous photocatalysts containing the light-absorbing moiety benzothiadiazole and consisting of a donor-acceptor architecture: a 3D cage (Cage) and a 2D macrocycle (MAC). Both photocatalysts generate H2O2 via the oxygen reduction reaction. Experimental studies revealed that the cage exhibits a higher photoactivity and catalytic performance than the macrocycle despite having a smaller surface area (29.2 m2/g). Even with no scavengers, Cage and MAC both yielded H2O2 at a rate of 483 µmol/g/h and 408 µmol/g/h, respectively, while introducing a hole scavenger, notably triethanolamine, resulted in a significant increase to 4208 µmol/g/h and 3018 µmol/g/h, respectively, after 6 hours of irradiation. articles.summary_en: Researchers developed benzothiadiazole-based porous organic photocatalysts that generate hydrogen peroxide from water and oxygen under light. A 3D cage outperformed a 2D macrocycle, reaching 4,208 µmol/g/h with triethanolamine as a hole scavenger.

articles.title_original: Lattice composite Fermi liquid with broken inversion symmetry
articles.title_en: Broken inversion symmetry reveals new transport signatures in graphene composite Fermi liquids
articles.excerpt_original: We study transport in lattice composite Fermi liquids realized in half-filled Chern bands with broken inversion symmetry. We show that reduced crystalline symmetry exposes intrinsic singular dynamical responses of composite fermions that are otherwise hidden in the conventional Landau-level setting. At zero wave vector, inversion breaking allows gauge-field fluctuations to generate a non-analytic longitudinal optical resistivity, with $\operatorname{Re}ρ^{xx}(ω)\sim |ω|^{4/3}$ for gate-screened Coulomb interactions. At finite wave vector $\mathbf{q}$, inversion breaking leads to nonreciprocal transport and a non-analytic $\sim |\mathbf{q}|$ dependence of the Hall conductivity, both of which can be probed through surface acoustic wave propagation. We also discuss a distinct mechanism for singular DC transport in lattice composite Fermi liquids: renormalization of $2k_F$ scattering at the composite Fermi surface enhances Umklapp relaxation and can lead to a non-analytic temperature dependence of the resistivity. Taken together, our results identify transport signatures of lattice composite Fermi liquids that are absent in their continuum quantum Hall counterparts and can be directly tested in ongoing experiments on twisted MoTe$_2$ and rhombohedral graphene, where evidence for zero-field composite Fermi liquids has recently been reported.
articles.summary_en: The study predicts non-analytic optical resistivity, nonreciprocal transport, and unusual temperature-dependent resistivity in lattice composite Fermi liquids with broken inversion symmetry. These signatures could be tested in twisted MoTe₂ and rhombohedral graphene, where zero-field composite Fermi liquids have been reported.

articles.title_original: An iterative method bridging DFT, disorder averaging, and experiment in intercalated materials: application to Au-intercalated graphene
articles.title_en: Iterative DFT–Experiment Method Models Au-Intercalated Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Intercalation can strongly modify the electronic dispersion of a host material, as directly revealed by angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES). We develop a general iterative method combining density functional theory (DFT), tight-binding (TB), disorder averaging within the self-consistent T-matrix approximation (SCTMA), and experiment, to construct an effective model of the intercalated system. DFT identifies the relevant microscopic degrees of freedom and constrains selected model parameters, while comparison of SCTMA calculations with experiment guides their further refinement. We apply this method to graphene intercalated with Au clusters and show that it reproduces the main ARPES signatures of the Au-cluster phase, including the broadening of the V12an Hove singularity and the emergence of kink-like features in the dispersion. The essential microscopic ingredients identified by the analysis are the hybridization between selected intercalant orbitals and the graphene states, together with an intercalation-induced local scattering potential.
articles.summary_en: Researchers present an iterative framework combining DFT, tight-binding, disorder averaging, and ARPES to model intercalated materials. Applied to graphene containing Au clusters, the method reproduces key spectral features and identifies orbital hybridization and local scattering as essential mechanisms.

articles.title_original: Two‐Dimensional Isotropic Spatial Differentiation Through Complete Polarization Control
articles.title_en: Polarization-Controlled Method Enables Isotropic Optical Edge Detection Across Broad Angles
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Optical image processing has emerged as an alternative to digital processing due to its high speed and reduced electronic burden. Among its various functions, spatial differentiation is particularly important because it provides essential structural information for image analysis. Reflection at planar interfaces enables two‐dimensional (2D) isotropic spatial differentiation without nanofabrication. However, previous demonstrations of this approach have been limited to specific incident conditions, such as the Brewster angle or a specific angle under total internal reflection at a lossless dielectric interface. Here, we demonstrate, via complete polarization control, that 2D isotropic edge detection at planar interfaces can be achieved over a wide range of incident angles by extending the output polarization from linear to elliptical. The resulting transfer function exhibits a linear amplitude profile and a first‐order phase vortex, corresponding to isotropic first‐order spatial differentiation. Relaxing the incident‐angle restriction allows the angle to be chosen to achieve desired performance, with near‐normal incidence being advantageous over a broad spectral range and large angles being favorable for higher edge‐detection efficiency. The 2D isotropic edge detection is experimentally verified using a BK7 prism and further extended to a metal‐coated mirror, showing that our principle remains valid for both dielectric and metallic reflective interfaces.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrate two-dimensional isotropic spatial differentiation at planar interfaces over a wide range of incident angles by using elliptical polarization control. Experiments with a BK7 prism and metal-coated mirror indicate potential for more flexible, efficient optical image-processing systems without nanofabrication.

articles.title_original: Drumhead Surface States of Rhombohedral Graphite with Near Ideal Quantum Geometry Condition
articles.title_en: Rhombohedral graphite study identifies topological drumhead surface states and ideal quantum geometry
articles.excerpt_original: The ideal quantum geometry (IQG) condition of equal magnitude between quantum metric ($G(k)$) and Berry curvature ($Ω(k)$) as in $|Ω|$/Tr$G$=1 has been associated with realizing fractional Chern insulators for the flat band in few layers of rhombohedral graphene (RG). More recently the IQG condition has also been proposed for superconductivity in the flat band for thick RG layers. Using density functional theory and Wannier functions, we study the symmetry-protected topology of bulk RG, drumhead surface state (DSS) of semi-infinite RG surface, and the IQG condition for thick RG slabs. We find that bulk RG is a weak topological insulator with spin-orbit coupling (SOC), besides being effectively a chiral semimetal with chiral nodal line without SOC. We also find that the DSS flat band of semi-infinite and thick RG slabs have a sizable convex curvature with depth agreeing with the recent angular resolved phono-emission spectroscopy experiment. The calculated IQG also shows a convex shape with the K point at the center having a minimum with approximately $|Ω|$/Tr$G$$\approx$1. But the inner rim of the DSS region shows the strict IQG condition of $|Ω|$/Tr$G$=1. These results on semi-infinite and thick RG slabs from first-principles calculations provide useful information for the pristine DSS at the single particle level for future studies to consider when many-body interactions and strong correlations will be included.
articles.summary_en: First-principles calculations show that rhombohedral graphite is a weak topological insulator with spin–orbit coupling and supports curved, nearly flat drumhead surface bands. The findings clarify quantum-geometry conditions relevant to future studies of correlated states, including fractional Chern insulators and superconductivity.

articles.title_original: Semi-Dirac semi-metals quantum dots
articles.title_en: Theoretical Study of Semi-Dirac Graphene Quantum Dots
articles.excerpt_original: Novel findings on nanostructures in semi-metal and semi-graphene materials are discussed regarding rectangular quantum dots with zigzag edges, MIT bag models, and Dirichlet boundary conditions. The article theoretically investigates some models of quantum dots for these hybrid materials and the point spectra of the semi-Dirac semi-Laplacians via one-dimensional Laplace and Dirac operators. We also prove the self-adjointness of the semi-Laplacian defined on a rectangle, subject to zigzag and hard-wall boundary conditions, and study its spectral properties.
articles.summary_en: An arXiv study theoretically examines rectangular quantum dots in semi-metal and semi-graphene materials with zigzag edges and hard-wall or Dirichlet boundary conditions. It analyzes spectral properties and proves self-adjointness for the associated semi-Laplacian operators.

articles.title_en: Gold intercalation modifies graphene standing waves and QPI
articles.excerpt_original: Gold intercalation beneath epitaxial graphene on SiC produces a cluster phase with unusual standing waves and quasiparticle-interference (QPI) features concentrated near the graphene M points. We show that this can be explained by Au intercalation below graphene hollow sites, which induces a local scattering potential on the six surrounding carbon atoms. Within a T-matrix treatment, this ring-like scatterer produces elliptical QPI structures centered near M, in agreement with the experimental FT-STS measurements. We further show that these QPI features naturally generate the nearly stationary standing-wave patterns observed in real space. Finally, we compute the local-density-of-states contrast on and off a small cluster and show that its sign and magnitude are strongly energy dependent, consistent with the experimental observations.
articles.summary_en: Researchers model how gold clusters intercalated beneath epitaxial graphene on SiC generate elliptical quasiparticle-interference structures near graphene’s M points. The findings explain observed standing-wave patterns and energy-dependent local-density-of-states contrast around gold clusters.

articles.title_original: Tunable Conformal Graphene Growth on Oxide Nanotube scaffolds: Towards Superwettable Hierarchical 2D-3D Architectures
articles.title_en: Plasma-Grown Graphene Nanowalls Enable Omniphobic Oxide Nanotube Surfaces
articles.excerpt_original: Hierarchical hybrid nanoarchitectures that integrate vertically oriented graphene nanowalls, GNWs, with metal oxide, MeOx, nanotube scaffolds offer versatile platform for smart surfaces, nanoelectronics, and electrochemical technologies. Herein we present rapid, dry, plasma-assisted fabrication route that enables direct and conformal growth of GNWs on mechanically robust MeOx nanoforests. The method combines supported single-crystalline organic nanowires as a 1D soft template with sequential plasma-enabled oxide deposition and GNW growth, all performed under mild temperature, power, and vacuum conditions. This approach yields an unprecedented 2D-3D hierarchical architecture consisting of tunable-thickness MeOx nanotubes uniformly decorated with radially oriented graphene nanosheets, forming re-entrant, multiscale surface. Resulting hierarchical roughness imparts fluorine-free, long-term omniphobicity, with contact angles exceeding 170 degree for water, bovine serum, and other complex fluids. GNWs dominate the wetting response across TiO2, Al2O3, and SiO2 nanotube scaffolds, effectively decoupling surface behavior from intrinsic oxide chemistry and maintaining robust repellency under UV irradiation and water condensation. Comprehensive SEM, TEM, XPS, angle-resolved NEXAFS, and Raman analyses elucidate growth mechanism and confirm preservation of the sp2 graphitic framework, together with controlled degree of edge functionalization. Overall, this work establishes universal, substrate-compatible, low-temperature, and scalable route for the fabrication of tunable graphene-metal oxide nano-microstructured multifunctional surfaces.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a low-temperature, plasma-assisted method for conformal growth of vertically oriented graphene nanowalls on TiO₂, Al₂O₃, and SiO₂ nanotube scaffolds. The resulting hierarchical surfaces reportedly achieved fluorine-free omniphobicity, with contact angles above 170°, while offering a scalable route to multifunctional coatings and interfaces.
