articles.title_original: Preparation of polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF)-graphene nanocomposites for energy storage applications
articles.title_en: PVDF–Graphene Nanocomposites for Energy Storage
articles.summary_en: Academic research examines preparation of polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF)–graphene nanocomposites for energy-storage applications. Available information does not specify performance results, device demonstrations, or commercialization prospects.

articles.title_original: Large-area CVD Graphene for Photogating-Based Photodetection
articles.title_en: Large-Area CVD Graphene Demonstrates High-Sensitivity Photogating Photodetection
articles.excerpt_original: Our work explores large-area CVD graphene as a scalable platform for photodetectors. We show that substrate-induced photogating in graphene/SiO$_2$/Si structures enables a photoconductivity signal in mono-, bi-, and trilayer CVD graphene. The devices respond to illumination with photon energies above the Si band gap and do not respond to telecom frequency, suggesting the photoconductivity mechanism through the photogating. Large sample area and gate voltage-dependent resistivity measurements allow us to prove the dominant role of the photogating directly, demonstrating similarity of the capacitive recharging current and the photoresponse. The sensitivity is the highest (995 A/W) for the monolayer graphene. Increasing the number of graphene layers reduces the sensitivity due to screening and parallel conduction, but can improve detectivity by lowering the noise level. The sensitivity of CVD graphene device depends on fabrication route of photolitography: device with metal contacts fabricated before graphene transfer show higher photoresponce. Thus, our work demonstrate the potential of industrially relevant CVD graphene for sensitive photogating-based photodetectors.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrate photogating-based photodetection in mono-, bi-, and trilayer CVD graphene on SiO₂/Si, with monolayer devices reaching 995 A/W sensitivity. The results support scalable CVD graphene for sensitive photodetectors, while layer number and contact fabrication affect sensitivity and detectivity.

articles.title_original: Synthesis, Structural Characteristics, and Applications of Vertically Oriented Graphene: A Review
articles.title_en: Review Assesses Vertically Oriented Graphene Synthesis and Applications
articles.excerpt_original: Vertically oriented graphene (VG), few-layer graphene nanosheets that stand upright on the substrate, has attracted significant attention within the carbon nanomaterial family owing to its unusual structural geometry and the resulting electrochemical and physical performance advantages. This review provides a comparative analysis of the two dominant synthesis routes: thermal chemical vapor deposition (Thermal CVD) and plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD). The plasma sheath electric field is identified as the key mechanism responsible for deterministic vertical growth. The roles of principal process parameters (plasma power density, gas composition, chamber pressure, and substrate bias) in shaping nanosheet morphology and crystallinity are examined. Applications of VG in electrochemical energy storage, high-sensitivity sensing, cold-cathode field emission, and electrocatalysis are surveyed. Outstanding challenges, including large-area uniformity, low-temperature growth, and long-term stability, are discussed alongside emerging trajectories such as machine-learning-driven process optimization and engineered two-dimensional heterostructures. Together, these discussions yield a coherent structure–property–function picture of VG that underpins its push toward practical device deployment.
articles.summary_en: A review compares thermal CVD and PECVD routes for vertically oriented graphene, identifying plasma-sheath electric fields as central to vertical growth and examining how process parameters affect morphology and crystallinity. It surveys applications in energy storage, sensing, cold-cathode field emission, and electrocatalysis while highlighting challenges in uniformity, low-temperature growth, and stability.

articles.title_original: Strain rate dependent performance of graphene-reinforced concrete: An experimental study
articles.title_en: Graphene Reinforces Concrete Under Dynamic Loading
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Graphene has been extensively studied due to its unique and exceptional combination of properties that promise revolutionary applications across many fields. While graphene has demonstrated its promise in improving the mechanical properties of concrete under quasi-static loading, the research on its effectiveness under dynamic loading is limited. This study addresses this gap by investigating the reinforcing effects of graphene on the mechanical behaviour of concrete under both quasi-static and dynamic loadings. Different graphene contents were added to the concrete mixes to assess their impact on compressive, splitting tensile, and flexural strengths of concrete. Quasi-static tests were conducted using a universal testing machine, while dynamic tests were carried out using a split Hopkinson pressure bar (SHPB) and a drop-weight hammer. The results revealed that the addition of 0.1% graphene to the concrete significantly enhanced both the quasi-static and dynamic compressive, splitting tensile, and flexural strengths, as well as the flexural energy absorption. The strain rate effects were also characterised using the dynamic increase factor (DIF). Moreover, microstructural analysis using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy-dispersive spectrometer (EDS), and mercury intrusion porosimeter (MIP) revealed the mechanisms of microstructural crack formation and propagation, providing insights into the macro-scale mechanical behaviour of graphene-reinforced concrete. The results highlight the potential of graphene to significantly enhance the mechanical properties of concrete under both quasi-static and high strain rate loadings, offering valuable implications for the design and construction of structures exposed to dynamic loading conditions.
articles.summary_en: An experimental study found that adding 0.1% graphene significantly improved concrete’s compressive, splitting tensile, and flexural strengths under both quasi-static and high-strain-rate loading. The results indicate potential for graphene-reinforced concrete in structures exposed to impact or other dynamic loads.

articles.title_original: Direct Observation of Flat Bands in Near-Magic-Angle Twisted Bilayer CVD Graphene
articles.title_en: Flat Bands Observed in Near-Magic-Angle CVD Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Advances in chemical vapor deposition (CVD) growth have driven graphene crystal quality to unprecedented levels, yet it is still unknown whether this route can realize the fragile flat-band and correlated states of the magic-angle (MA) twisted bilayer graphene (TBG). Here, we report on the experimental observation by room-temperature nano-angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (nano-ARPES) of flat bands in a TBG sample close to the MA, assembled via a grow-and-stack protocol based on low-pressure CVD of graphene on copper. Our study indicates electronic bands fully comparable to those measured in exfoliation-based samples and determines the size of the largest near-MA domain to be compatible with electronic transport experiments, motivating further experiments on flat-band physics in CVD-graphene.
articles.summary_en: Researchers directly observed flat bands in near-magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene produced by low-pressure CVD on copper. The results show electronic properties comparable to exfoliated samples and support further investigation of correlated-state physics in scalable CVD graphene.

articles.title_original: The role of surface chemistry in V₂C MXenes for biomolecular recognition: a DFT study on dopamine and DNA nucleobases
articles.title_en: DFT study examines V₂C MXene surface chemistry for biomolecular recognition
articles.summary_en: A density-functional-theory study investigates how V₂C MXene surface chemistry affects interactions with dopamine and DNA nucleobases. The findings may inform MXene-based biosensors and biomedical recognition platforms, but no commercial application is reported.

articles.title_original: V2C MXene nanosheets and Au particles-decorated boron-doped diamond electrodes for non-enzymatic glucose sensing
articles.title_en: MXene–Gold Diamond Electrode Enables Non-Enzymatic Glucose Sensing
articles.excerpt_original: Non-enzymatic glucose sensors are attractive alternatives to enzyme-based systems due to their improved chemical stability, but their analytical performance depends heavily on electrode surface design. In this work, a hybrid electrode based on V 2 C MXene and gold (Au) particles supported on boron-doped diamond (BDD) was fabricated and evaluated for electrochemical glucose detection. V 2 C MXene was obtained by selective etching of V 2 AlC, producing a layered and conductive coating on the BDD surface. Subsequent deposition of Au particles introduced additional catalytic sites for glucose oxidation. Structural and surface characterization confirmed the formation of V 2 C MXene, preservation of carbide bonding, and the presence of metallic Au. Electrochemical measurements in phosphate-buffered saline showed that the BDD-V 2 C-Au electrode exhibited a sensitivity of 24.14 μA ppm −1 cm −2 , a detection limit of 0.15 ppm, and a linear response over the concentration range from 0.18 to 125 ppm. Compared with the BDD-V 2 C electrode, Au modification led to a significant enhancement in current response. The electrode also showed good repeatability and short-term stability in different supporting electrolytes. When compared with representative non-enzymatic glucose sensors reported in the literature, the BDD-V 2 C-Au provided a well-defined balance between sensitivity, detection limit, and operational stability. These results highlight the potential of MXene-noble metal interfaces on diamond substrates for stable, non-enzymatic glucose sensing under controlled conditions.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a boron-doped diamond electrode decorated with V2C MXene nanosheets and gold particles for electrochemical glucose detection. The hybrid electrode achieved 24.14 μA ppm−1 cm−2 sensitivity, a 0.15 ppm detection limit, and short-term operational stability under controlled conditions.

articles.title_original: Microstructure and Properties of Surface Modification of Hexagonal Boron Nitride and Carbon Nanotubes/Magnesium Composites
articles.title_en: h-BN Surface Modification Improves Magnesium–CNT Composite Properties
articles.excerpt_original: In order to enhance the wettability and scattering between matrix and reinforcement, the effects of incorporating hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) into magnesium-carbon nanotubes (Mg-0.5 weight percent CNTs) nanocomposites were successfully investigated for the first time in this paper. This was accomplished by means of an inventive electroless chemical deposition technique and double stirs casting. The composites were produced using varying weight percentages of h-BN (0 and 2wt%). On the produced sample&s;s tribological testing, microstructural analysis, hardness values were elucidated. Wear rate and hardness were all improved when the 2 weight percent of h-BN content was compared to Mg-0.5%wtCNTs-0%h-BN. The result shows that a combination of electroless deposition and double stir casting methods can effectively develop impressive nanoparticle-coated Mg-CNTs/h-BN nanocomposites.
articles.summary_en: Researchers investigated electroless deposition and double-stir casting to incorporate hexagonal boron nitride into magnesium–carbon nanotube composites. Adding 2 wt% h-BN improved hardness and wear resistance, indicating a potential route to enhanced tribological performance.

articles.title_original: First-principles and molecular dynamics insights into interfacial interactions of CrTe2/h-BN van der Waals heterostructures for enhanced anchoring in magnesium-ion batteries
articles.title_en: Study explores CrTe2/h-BN interfaces for improved magnesium-ion battery anchoring
articles.summary_en: First-principles calculations and molecular dynamics simulations examine interfacial interactions in CrTe2/h-BN van der Waals heterostructures. The findings indicate potential for stronger anchoring in magnesium-ion battery systems, but remain at the academic research stage.

articles.title_original: Surface-modified h-BN suppresses thermal-oxidative degradation of synthetic ester oil-paper insulation through interfacial hydronium-ion regulation
articles.title_en: Surface-Modified h-BN Improves Synthetic Ester Oil-Paper Insulation Aging
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Thermal-oxidative aging of synthetic ester oil-paper insulation is closely associated with acid-catalyzed depolymerization of cellulose, in which hydronium ions play a key role at the oil-paper interface. In this work, KH550-modified hexagonal boron nitride (KH550-hBN) nanoparticles were introduced into a synthetic ester oil-paper insulation system to examine whether the nanoparticle interface can regulate the interaction and transport behavior of hydronium ions during aging. Accelerated thermal aging was carried out at 155 °C in air, and the evolution of acid value, dielectric loss, AC breakdown strength, tensile strength, and degree of polymerization (DP) was evaluated. Compared with the unmodified system, the nanomodified system showed lower dielectric loss and acid value, while the DP of the impregnated paper remained 13.5% higher after 672 h of aging. Kinetic analysis based on the DP data further showed that the cellulose degradation rate constant decreased by 21.1% after nanoparticle incorporation. SEM observations confirmed that the modified paper retained a more intact fiber morphology with fewer cracks after prolonged aging. To clarify the underlying mechanism, molecular dynamics simulations were performed using the Universal force field. The results showed that KH550-hBN weakens the interaction between cellulose and hydronium ions, reduces hydrogen-bond formation between them, and suppresses hydronium-ion diffusion. These findings indicate that the functionalized nanoparticle interface reduces both the tendency of hydronium ions to approach cellulose and their mobility near the oil-paper interface, thereby slowing acid-catalyzed cellulose degradation. This work provides a mechanism-based explanation for the improved aging stability of nanomodified est
articles.summary_en: KH550-functionalized hexagonal boron nitride nanoparticles reduced hydronium-ion diffusion and acid-catalyzed cellulose degradation in synthetic ester oil-paper insulation during accelerated thermal aging. After 672 hours, impregnated paper retained 13.5% higher polymerization degree and showed lower acid value and dielectric loss than unmodified insulation.

articles.title_original: Flexible AlGaN/GaN HEMT devices exfoliated from Si substrate by electrochemical etching
articles.title_en: Electrochemical etching enables flexible AlGaN/GaN HEMT transfer
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Flexible electronic/optoelectronic devices based on wide-bandgap materials are gaining great attention due to the demand of versatile commercial and military applications. This paper presents an electrochemical etching technique for high-quality transfer of AlGaN/GaN high-electron-mobility transistor (HEMT) thin films from silicon substrate to temporary substrates. Unlike conventional mechanical grinding, this method avoids mechanical damage to the device, thereby preserving the structural integrity and electrical properties of the heterostructure. The surface morphology of the exfoliated HEMT thin films was confirmed by atomic force microscopy (AFM) images with a root mean square (RMS) roughness of 1.9 nm. This transfer technique offers a wafer-scale and low-damage route for fabricating high-performance flexible III-nitride semiconductor devices for wearable, radio-frequency, and power applications.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrate wafer-scale, low-damage transfer of AlGaN/GaN HEMT thin films from silicon to temporary substrates using electrochemical etching. The method preserves device integrity and electrical properties, supporting flexible semiconductor devices for wearable, radio-frequency, and power applications.

articles.title_original: Overcoming the temperature limitation of lithium-ion batteries: Local dynamics in supported ionic liquid–polymer electrolytes
articles.title_en: PAN-Supported Ionic-Liquid Electrolyte Enables High-Temperature Lithium-Ion Batteries
articles.excerpt_original: Lithium-ion batteries designed for operation under harsh conditions require electrolytes that mitigate the volatility, flammability, and thermal instability of organic electrolytes. In this work, we study a high-temperature supported polymer electrolyte based on the tetrabutylphosphonium (trifluoromethylnonafluorobutylsulfonyl) imide (P4444IM14) ionic liquid with the LiTFSI salt, confined within polyacrylonitrile (PAN) membrane. Ion dynamics were studied using multinuclear NMR, combining diffusion and FFC-NMR on 1H, 19F, and 7Li, complemented by solid-state 13C NMR of the PAN host. PFG-NMR shows that LiTFSI reduces ionic self-diffusion in the liquid electrolyte, while incorporation into the PAN membrane does not further limit diffusion. Consistently, NMRD profiles remain essentially unchanged upon confinement with the polymer membrane, with no evidence of additional relaxation mechanisms associated with confinement, indicating weak dynamic coupling at the polymer–electrolyte interface. Thermal and electrochemical properties were also investigated confirming minimal influence of the PAN on electrolyte performance. Graphical Abstract
articles.summary_en: Researchers studied a tetrabutylphosphonium ionic-liquid/LiTFSI electrolyte confined in a polyacrylonitrile membrane for high-temperature lithium-ion battery operation. NMR results indicate that PAN confinement does not significantly impair ion diffusion or electrolyte thermal and electrochemical performance.

articles.title_original: A Unified Machine‐Learning Framework for Predicting Barrier‐Free Metal Contacts in 2D Semiconductor Transistors
articles.title_en: Machine-learning framework screens barrier-free metal contacts for 2D transistors
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Achieving low‐resistance, reproducible metal contacts remains a major obstacle to integrating two‐dimensional (2D) semiconductors into deeply scaled CMOS technologies. Despite intensive study of selected semiconductor‐metal (S‐M) interfaces, particularly those based on transition‐metal dichalcogenides, contact optimization continues to rely heavily on experimental, and computational trial‐and‐error, in part due to variations in interface structure and processing that obscure intrinsic trends and hinder direct comparison. To address this challenge, we present a unified, data‐driven framework that connects atomistic interface physics with device‐level metrics using descriptor‐light machine learning. Based on high‐throughput density‐functional‐theory (DFT) calculations spanning 16 665 candidate 2D semiconductors and 80 metals, we construct a record‐scale dataset covering diverse interface chemistries and contact regimes. Trained solely on publicly available database‐derived elemental descriptors, the models predict van der Waals (vdW) barrier formation together with vertical, and lateral Schottky barrier heights (SBHs) within milliseconds, enabling rapid, ab initio‐free screening of arbitrary contacts. Validation against experimental data and quantum transport simulations confirms accurate reproduction of established contact behaviors and resistance trends. The framework further identifies over one hundred previously unexplored near‐barrier‐free interfaces and reveals physically interpretable principles governing carrier injection, establishing a scalable pathway toward intrinsically Ohmic 2D contacts.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a machine-learning framework trained on 16,665 2D semiconductors and 80 metals to predict contact barriers and Schottky barrier heights. Validated against experimental and quantum-transport data, the approach identifies more than 100 unexplored near-barrier-free interfaces for potentially lower-resistance CMOS contacts.

articles.title_original: Identifying Contact Barrier Types in Few-Layer MoS2 Devices Using Correlative IV, LBIC, and Bias-Dependent KPFM
articles.title_en: Correlative Method Identifies Contact Barriers in Few-Layer MoS₂ Devices
articles.excerpt_original: Electrical contacts between metals and two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors such as molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) critically govern device performance, yet their microscopic nature remains difficult to disentangle using any single characterization technique. Here we present an integrated experimental framework that combines current-voltage (IV) characterization, laser beam induced current (LBIC) mapping, and bias-dependent Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) to comprehensively resolve the contact properties of few-layer MoS2-based two-terminal devices under ambient conditions. IV measurements deliver macroscopic transport characteristics as a function of bias voltage and illumination conditions. LBIC maps the local photocurrent response with micrometer spatial resolution, revealing the position and nature of internal electric fields at MoS2-metal interfaces. KPFM, operated under an applied static bias rather than in the conventional work-function mode, provides nanoscale-resolved potential distributions that quantify the relative magnitudes and spatial locations of contact barriers. We apply this framework to three representative devices - one exhibiting ohmic-like and two exhibiting diode-like contact behavior - and demonstrate that the combined analysis can unambiguously identify whether the dominant barrier is of Schottky or tunnel type and determine the asymmetry between the two contacts. We further demonstrate that thermal annealing significantly reduces the total resistance, while contact barriers remain the dominant source of resistance. The methodology is directly transferable to other 2D semiconductor-metal systems and provides a practical yet comprehensive route toward a quantitative microscopic understanding of 2D device contacts.
articles.summary_en: Researchers combined IV measurements, laser-induced photocurrent mapping and bias-dependent KPFM to distinguish Schottky and tunnel barriers in MoS₂–metal contacts. The study found that annealing reduces overall resistance, but contact barriers remain the main resistance source, offering a transferable characterization method for 2D semiconductor devices.

articles.title_original: Multistate control in 2D CuCrP2S6/Sc2CO2 multiferroic heterostructures
articles.title_en: 2D heterostructure enables four-state spintronic memory control
articles.excerpt_original: The magnetoelectric (ME) coupling effect enables effective cross-control between electric and magnetic fields, providing a crucial pathway toward next-generation low-power electronic devices. Here, we propose a two-dimensional (2D) multistate multiferroic heterostructure (MMH) composed of out-of-plane polarized CuCrP2S6 and Sc2CO2 (CCPS/SCO) to realize electric field driven multistate spintronic devices. First-principles calculations demonstrate that the CCPS/SCO heterostructure can be reversibly switched among four nonvolatile polarization states (↑↑, ↑↓, ↓↓, ↓↑) using electrical pulses, enabling simultaneous control of electronic transport, magnetic ordering, and spin orientation within a single heterostructure. By encoding the four polarization states, three distinct quantum phases are identified, i.e., out-of-plane antiferromagnetic metal, in-plane ferromagnetic semiconductor, and out-of-plane ferromagnetic metal. The microscopic mechanism underlying this strong ME coupling originates from polarization-induced interfacial charge transfer and symmetry breaking, which synergistically shift the energy level and tune the orbital occupation of Cr-d orbitals. Our proposed CCPS/SCO MMH heterostructure establishes a promising platform for high-density, low-power, and functionally reconfigurable spintronic memory.
articles.summary_en: First-principles calculations propose a CuCrP2S6/Sc2CO2 heterostructure that can be electrically switched among four nonvolatile polarization states. The states enable control of transport, magnetism and spin orientation, supporting reconfigurable, low-power spintronic memory concepts.

articles.title_original: Hybrid metal-semiconductor quantum dots in InAs as a platform for quantum simulation
articles.title_en: Hybrid InAs Metal–Semiconductor Quantum Dots Proposed for Quantum Simulation
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Arrays of hybrid metal-semiconductor quantum dots offer a new approach to quantum simulation, with key advantages over arrays of conventional quantum dots. Because the metallic component of these hybrid dots has a quasi-continuous level spectrum, each site in an array can be effectively electronically identical; in contrast, each conventional semiconductor quantum dot has its own spectral fingerprint. Meanwhile, the semiconductor component retains gate-tunability of intersite coupling. This combination creates a scalable platform for simulating correlated ground states driven by Coulomb interactions. We report the fabrication and characterization of hybrid metal-semiconductor dots, featuring a submicron metal island transparently contacting a gate-confined region of an InAs quantum well with tunable couplings to macroscopic leads. Tuning the dot-lead coupling to the weak-coupling limit yields highly-uniform Coulomb peaks, with no resolvable excitation spectrum in the Coulomb diamonds. We propose a realistic device design for a hybrid dot-based linear array quantum simulator and outline the correlated many-body physics accessible in this architecture.
articles.summary_en: Researchers fabricated and characterized hybrid metal–semiconductor quantum dots combining a metallic island with a gate-confined InAs quantum well. The platform provides uniform Coulomb peaks and tunable coupling, supporting scalable simulation of correlated many-body states.

articles.title_original: A Refined 2D Simulation Framework: EPR Optimization for Superconducting Qubit with Process-Realistic Geometry
articles.title_en: Process-realistic 2D simulations optimize superconducting qubit coherence
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Energy participation ratio (EPR) at the metal-substrate interface is a dominant decoherence source limiting the coherence time (T1) of planar superconducting transmon qubits. Traditional EPR simulations rely on idealized geometric models, ignoring process-induced morphological deviations that significantly impact actual device performance. To bridge this gap, we propose a unified data-driven framework. It automatically extracts geometric parameters from SEM cross-sections using computer vision (CV). These parameters are then imported into a calibrated 2D EPR simulation model. Sobol global sensitivity analysis is further applied to quantify the influences of key parameters. Parametric simulations reveal that the EPR scaling factor Fms generally decreases with increasing interface thickness, substrate over-etch depth, and trench angle, driven by mitigated edge electric field crowding. Sobol analysis further identifies substrate over-etch depth and trench angle as the dominant drivers of Fms, with a significant synergistic interaction between these two parameters. Evaluations across eight process-feasible geometric configurations indicate that thin interface layer combined with a deep substrate over-etch yields the largest predict reduction in interface EPR, corresponding to a projected relative enhancement in T1 under the assumption of a constant interface loss tangent. We derive actionable process guidelines for planar Al-on-Si transmon qubits, prioritizing the co-tuning of trench parameters to balance MS-interface EPR reduction with manufacturing feasibility within the investigated parameter range. This framework provides a systematic pipeline for incorporating process-induced geometric deviations into EPR prediction, and offers a design-stage simulation tool a
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a data-driven framework that combines SEM-based geometry extraction with calibrated 2D energy participation ratio simulations for planar superconducting transmons. The study identifies substrate over-etch depth and trench angle as dominant factors in reducing interface losses and improving projected T1 performance.

articles.title_original: Hydrogel‐Enabled Electrochemical Modulation of 2D Single‐Crystalline VO <sub>2</sub> Films for Flexible Neuromorphic Electronics
articles.title_en: Hydrogel-Gated 2D VO₂ Devices Enable Flexible Neuromorphic Electronics
articles.excerpt_original: Electrolyte‐gated transistors (EGTs) based on strongly correlated oxides show great promise as artificial synaptic devices due to their ionic–electronic coupling, which allows for significant conductance modulation, low‐bias operation, and long‐lasting memory states. However, there has been limited exploration of platelet‐based two‐dimensional (2D) crystalline VO 2 channels that can simultaneously achieve nonvolatile conductance programming, array‐level addressability, and flexible neuromorphic functionality. In this study, we present hydrogel‐gated EGTs utilizing chemical‐vapor‐deposition‐grown 2D‐crystalline VO 2 platelet channels. These devices exhibit sub‐1 V conductance programming, nonvolatile state retention, and reversible write–retain–erase capabilities at both the single‐device and 4 × 6 array levels. Spectroscopic analyses provide strong evidence for proton‐coupled electrochemical modulation within the VO 2 channel. Building on this programmable correlated‐oxide platform, we demonstrate a variety of synaptic functions, including paired‐pulse facilitation, spike‐number‐dependent plasticity, spike‐rate‐dependent plasticity, long‐term potentiation/depression, and spike‐timing‐dependent plasticity. Furthermore, after being transferred to flexible substrates, the devices continue to exhibit robust analog potentiation/depression under tensile and compressive strain, as well as repeated bending. The experimentally determined synaptic weights also support stable handwritten‐digit recognition in a simulated neural network. These findings establish hydrogel‐gated 2D‐crystalline VO 2 EGTs as a mechanically compliant and array‐addressable correlated‐oxide platform for flexible neuromorphic electronics.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed hydrogel-gated electrolyte transistors using 2D single-crystalline VO₂ channels, achieving sub-1 V programming, nonvolatile memory, and array-level operation. The devices retained synaptic behavior under bending and tensile or compressive strain, supporting flexible neuromorphic computing applications.

articles.title_original: Non-Centrosymmetric $γ$-Phase GaS Nanobelts for On-Chip Nonlinear Photonic Applications
articles.title_en: γ-GaS Nanobelts Enable On-Chip Nonlinear Photonics
articles.excerpt_original: Second-order nonlinear optical processes in van der Waals (vdW) semiconductors offer a compelling route toward compact, integrable photon-conversion platforms. Among III-VI vdW semiconductors, GaS is particularly attractive owing to its wide bandgap suppressing two-photon absorption under near-infrared laser excitation. However, bulk GaS typically crystallizes in the centrosymmetric $β$ phase, which eliminates second-order nonlinearity and severely limits its application in nonlinear photonics. Here, we demonstrate that GaS nanobelts synthesized via self-catalyzed vapor-liquid-solid growth predominantly crystallize in non-centrosymmetric $γ$-phase stacking. This behavior originates from edge-selective growth kinetics at the Ga catalyst interface, which stabilizes the $γ$ phase and enables deterministic in-plane dipole moment alignment. The GaS nanobelts exhibit strong second-harmonic generation (SHG) with intensities comparable to those of GaSe, a widely used nonlinear optical material. Furthermore, we integrate the nanobelts onto SiN waveguides and demonstrate efficient on-chip SHG and sum-frequency generation. These results establish $γ$-GaS nanobelts as a transferable one-dimensional nonlinear materials well suited for on-chip photonic integration and indicate their strong potential for nonlinear optical applications.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated predominantly non-centrosymmetric γ-phase GaS nanobelts with strong second-harmonic generation. Integrated onto SiN waveguides, the nanobelts enabled on-chip second-harmonic and sum-frequency generation for compact photonic applications.

articles.title_original: Real-time exciton dynamics in two-dimensional materials under ultrashort laser pulses
articles.title_en: Study models real-time exciton dynamics in h-BN and GeS monolayers
articles.excerpt_original: The optical response of two-dimensional materials is often significantly impacted by excitonic effects due to the reduced screening of attractive Coulomb interactions in low-dimensional systems. Accurate modeling of exciton formation and real-time dynamics is essential to understanding their ultrafast optical properties. In this study, we theoretically investigate the exciton dynamics in a two-dimensional hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) and a germanium sulfide (GeS) monolayers exposed to an ultrashort laser pulse. We analyze the system's response to the external field in one- and two-photon excitation regimes. For our calculations, we combine a state-of-the-art approach to study exciton dynamics with a highly precise numerical scheme. We incorporate electron-hole interactions through a nonlocal self-energy operator derived from the many-body perturbation theory (MBPT) within the time-dependent adiabatic G W ( TD − a G W ) approximation. We implement this approach using the full-electron LAPW + lo method in the all-electron package. Our results elucidate the role of many-body effects in shaping ultrafast excitonic processes in two-dimensional materials, contributing to the fundamental understanding necessary for optoelectronic and photonic applications.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a many-body computational approach to analyze exciton formation and ultrafast dynamics in two-dimensional hexagonal boron nitride and germanium sulfide under one- and two-photon excitation. The findings advance fundamental understanding relevant to future optoelectronic and photonic devices, but report no commercial application or company involvement.

articles.title_original: Moiré effects in low-dimensional heterostructures: from 2D materials to 2D–3D mixed-dimensional systems
articles.title_en: Review maps moiré physics from graphene to mixed-dimensional systems
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Moiré superlattices provide a versatile means of modifying electronic bands through periodic potentials generated by lattice mismatch or rotational misalignment. Over the past decade, this concept has reshaped the study of low-dimensional quantum materials, enabling the observation of flat bands, correlated insulating behavior, unconventional superconductivity, excitonic states, and topological responses. More recently, moiré physics has begun to move beyond the conventional limit of atomically thin two-dimensional (2D) heterostructures. Experimental studies have shown that a moiré potential formed at a 2D interface can propagate into adjacent three-dimensional materials and reconstruct their bulk electronic states, giving rise to mixed-dimensional moiré systems. This review summarizes recent progress in moiré effects from 2D platforms to mixed-dimensional architectures. We first present the fundamental physical definition of moiré patterns and trace their historical development. We then review graphene-based moiré systems with different layer numbers, where twist-angle control modifies band dispersion, enhances electronic correlations, and leads to superconductivity near magic angles. The discussion is extended to transition metal dichalcogenide moiré heterostructures, with emphasis on excitonic physics, interlayer hybridization, correlation effects, and nontrivial band topology. We then focus on 2D–3D mixed-dimensional heterostructures, where interfacial moiré modulation penetrates into bulk materials and produces electronic reconstruction beyond the interface. Finally, we discuss future directions involving broader material choices, improved control over stacking and twist geometry, advanced probes of buried moiré potentials, and the search for unexplored co
articles.summary_en: The review surveys how lattice mismatch and twist angles modify electronic bands in graphene and other 2D heterostructures, enabling flat bands, correlated states, superconductivity, excitonic behavior, and topology. It also examines emerging 2D–3D systems in which interfacial moiré potentials reconstruct electronic states within adjacent bulk materials.

articles.title_original: Regulation of vacancy formation in h-BN via carbon doping toward improved resistive switching
articles.title_en: Carbon Doping Improves h-BN Resistive Switching
articles.excerpt_original: Hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) exhibits promising potential in resistive switching applications, yet the performance variability remains a major obstacle, primarily due to the uncontrollable nature of intrinsic defects. Carbon doping can offer a potential means to regulate defect types and their spatial distribution. However, the microscopic mechanisms by which carbon dopants regulate defects in h-BN remain unclear. In this work, the modulation of the resistive switching behavior in h-BN based RRAM by carbon dopants is studied using first-principles calculations. The results indicate that carbon substituted for boron (CB) not only promotes the formation of boron vacancies (VB), but its interaction with vacancies further facilitates vacancy clustering around the dopant. Notably, interlayer interactions depend on defect type, with in adjacent layers exhibiting mutual repulsion, whereas nitrogen vacancies (VN) attract and stabilize . Climbing image nudged elastic band (CI-NEB) calculations demonstrate that resistive switching does not rely on migration but is mediated by boron-nitrogen divacancy (VBN) enabled conductive bridge formation (-1q/-2q charge states) and breaking (0q/+1q charge states). Non-equilibrium Green's function (NEGF) transport calculations verify a pronounced enhancement of the current upon conductive bridge formation. This work provides fundamental theoretical insights for defect engineering in the development of h-BN based RRAM.
articles.summary_en: First-principles calculations show that carbon dopants regulate vacancy formation and clustering in hexagonal boron nitride, enabling more controlled conductive-bridge formation. articles.title_original: Hidden polymorphic landscape in two-dimensional ZnO
articles.title_en: Study Reveals Hidden Polymorphic Landscape in Two-Dimensional ZnO
articles.excerpt_original: Two-dimensional ZnO has long been described by a graphitic honeycomb model, yet growing experimental evidence suggests a more complex structural landscape. Here, we use physics-constrained random structure search and first-principles calculations to explore the low-energy configurations of monolayer ZnO. We find that the planar graphitic phase is not the ground state. Instead, ZnO favors a double-layer honeycomb structure stabilized by interlayer Zn–O bonds, which appears graphitic in projection but is chemically distinct from a planar sheet. We further uncover a family of metastable triangular–tetrahedral polymorphs located 40–56 meV/atom above the ground state. These phases are dynamically stable and arise from coupled electrostatic and coordination disproportionation, which redistributes electrostatic repulsion and splits distorted tetrahedral sites into trigonal and tetrahedral building blocks. These findings recast polar non-van der Waals semiconductors as competing structural landscapes shaped by polarity, coordination, and electrostatics.
articles.summary_en: AIP Publishing researchers used structure searches and first-principles calculations to show that monolayer ZnO may favor a double-layer honeycomb structure rather than the traditionally assumed planar graphitic phase. The study also identifies dynamically stable triangular–tetrahedral metastable polymorphs, offering new insight into structural design of two-dimensional semiconductor materials.

articles.title_original: Computational Insights into Polymer Binder–Graphene Interfaces: Chitosan-Functionalized Graphene Oxide as a Sustainable Platform for Lithium-Ion Batteries

In this work, density functional theory calculations were used to evaluate the interactions of representative binder monomers acrylonitrile (AN), pyrrole (PY), vinylidene fluoride (VDF), and tetrafluoroethylene (TFE) with pristine graphene and chitosan-functionalized graphene oxide (GO/chitosan). Structural, energetic, electronic, and topological features were analyzed using counterpoise-corrected interaction energies, frontier-orbital descriptors, molecular electrostatic potential maps, projected density of states, noncovalent interaction analysis, and quantum theory of atoms in molecules topology. Final interaction energies were obtained at the M06-2X/def2-TZVP level with Boys–Bernardi counterpoise correction to provide a more robust description of weak noncovalent adsorption. Most binder–surface interactions fall within a weak, near-thermoneutral adsorption regime. On pristine graphene, AN and PY exhibit weakly favorable adsorption, with minimum counterpoise-corrected interaction energies of −3.13 and −2.10 kcal mol−1, respectively, whereas TFE and VDF show orientation-dependent, near-neutral behavior. GO/chitosan introduces oxygen-containing and amino functionalities that modify the adsorption balance, particularly for selected perpendicular configurations of fluorinated monomers, although the net stabilization remains modest. NCI, QTAIM, MEP, and PDOS analyses indicate that surface functionalization increases the chemical heterogeneity and directionality of local contacts; however, these local descriptors do not necessarily translate into strong global adsorption energies. articles.summary_en: Computational analysis finds mostly weak, near-thermoneutral adsorption between representative binder monomers and graphene or chitosan-functionalized graphene oxide. Functionalization increases local chemical heterogeneity and contact directionality, but does not produce strong overall binding energies.

articles.title_original: Design and Optimization of High-G Graphene MEMS Acceleration Sensor
articles.title_en: Graphene MEMS Accelerometer Optimized for High-G Measurement
articles.excerpt_original: High-g accelerometers are in high demand across sectors such as aerospace, defense, and industrial inspection. This paper presents a MEMS accelerometer based on graphene piezoresistors, designed for precise acceleration measurement under sudden impacts, intense vibrations, and extreme conditions, such as engine fault diagnosis and weapon impact testing. A step-by-step structural optimization and simulation analysis were conducted using finite-element simulation. Taking the peak strain at the beam root, the first-order natural frequency, and the maximum equivalent stress as optimization objectives, progressive parametric optimization was sequentially performed on four progressive architectures: a simple beam, a beam mass, a beam mass with stress concentration grooves, and a beam mass with stress concentration grooves and symmetric masses. The results indicate that the introduction of a central mass enhances the peak strain by more than 15 times compared to the simple beam. The addition of stress concentration grooves further increases the strain by approximately 30%. Finally, the incorporation of symmetric masses yields a further 9% strain enhancement while reducing cross-axis sensitivity by 5.6%, effectively suppressing off-axis interference. The final structure achieves maximized strain while maintaining a first-order natural frequency above 200 kHz, with the maximum equivalent stress staying within the allowable limit. This optimal comprehensive performance provides essential technical support for high-performance graphene-based accelerometers. articles.summary_en: Researchers designed and simulated a graphene-piezoresistor MEMS accelerometer for high-impact and vibration environments relevant to aerospace, defense, and industrial inspection. Structural changes increased beam-root strain by more than 15-fold while maintaining a first-order natural frequency above 200 kHz and reducing cross-axis sensitivity.

articles.title_original: Deterministic Integration of Quantum Emitters and Optical Cavities in a Van Der Waals Crystal
articles.title_en: Deterministic Integration of hBN Quantum Emitters with Optical Cavities
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Single‐photon emitters in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) combine bright optical emission with optically addressable spin states, offering a promising platform for integrated quantum photonics. However, their stochastic creation and spectral variability have prevented deterministic integration with photonic cavities. Here we demonstrate a fabrication protocol that enables precise, deterministic coupling of pre‐selected visible emitters to circular Bragg grating (CBG) cavities in hBN. By patterning etched alignment markers and performing pre‐fabrication confocal mapping, we locate emitters with sub‐micron accuracy and design cavity geometries matched to their zero‐phonon line wavelengths. The resulting devices show enhanced emission and reliable spectral alignment between emitter and cavity mode. This work establishes a deterministic cavity‐emitter integration scheme in a van der Waals material and provides a scalable route toward on‐chip quantum photonic and spin‐based platforms using hBN.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a fabrication protocol to deterministically couple selected visible emitters in hexagonal boron nitride with circular Bragg grating cavities. articles.title_original: Exciton–phonon coupling in two-dimensional materials: from phenomena to applications
articles.title_en: Review Maps Exciton–Phonon Coupling in 2D Materials to Emerging Applications
articles.excerpt_original: Exciton–phonon coupling is a fundamental interaction governing the optical, electronic, and thermal properties of semiconductors. Two-dimensional (2D) materials, with reduced dielectric screening and strong confinement, exhibit enhanced exciton binding energies and exciton–phonon coupling, offering a rich platform for studying related phenomena. Here, we provide a brief review of exciton–phonon interactions in 2D materials. We first introduce the basic physical mechanisms, including the Huang–Rhys factor and different coupling regimes. Then, we summarize representative phenomena such as phonon-assisted upconversion, self-trapped excitons, exciton formation dynamics, and phonon-mediated dark-exciton processes. Next, we discuss exciton–spin–phonon coupling in van der Waals magnetic materials. Finally, we highlight emerging applications, including solid-state laser cooling, single-photon sources, and exciton-optomechanics, and provide perspectives on future research directions in this field.
articles.summary_en: A review examines how exciton–phonon interactions shape optical, electronic and thermal behavior in two-dimensional semiconductors, including phonon-assisted upconversion and dark-exciton processes. It highlights potential applications in solid-state laser cooling, single-photon sources and exciton optomechanics.

articles.title_original: Inverse Piezoelectricity and Carrier-Mediated Phase Instability as Intrinsic Limits in Two-Dimensional Transition Metal Dichalcogenide-Based Devices
articles.title_en: Intrinsic Failure Mechanisms Identified in 2D TMD FETs
articles.excerpt_original: planar FETs, revealing two competing intrinsic mechanisms that are qualitatively distinct from and largely undetected in conventional bulk semiconductor reliability physics. In carrier-depleted channels (field-dominant regime), strong out-of-plane electric fields in the absence of carriers trigger a dominant inverse piezoelectric effect, inducing compressive strain that dramatically lowers the formation energy for sulfur vacancies. This creates a runaway process where defects accumulate and initiate failure near the drain. Conversely, in carrier-rich channels (carrier-dominant regime), mobile electrons stabilize the semiconducting 2H to metallic 1T phase transition in the presence of dominant tensile strain due to an in-plane electric field, forming highly conductive filaments that burn through via Joule heating. Electrical measurements combined with Raman spectroscopy, photoluminescence, and scanning capacitance microscopy reveal diagnostic signatures distinguishing these pathways. These findings indicate that electrical degradation in 2D materials is strongly governed by material-specific properties, namely, piezoelectricity and phase stability, which are largely absent in bulk semiconductors. This framework enables predictive degradation models for other atomically thin materials with similar electromechanical coupling, establishing piezoelectricity and phase instability as defining intrinsic limits for nanoelectronic and quantum device engineering.
articles.summary_en: Research identifies two distinct degradation pathways in transition-metal dichalcogenide FETs: inverse-piezoelectric strain accelerates sulfur-vacancy formation in carrier-depleted channels, while carrier-mediated phase transitions create conductive filaments in carrier-rich channels. The findings support predictive reliability models for atomically thin nanoelectronic and quantum devices.

articles.title_original: Optical code division multiple access system using two-dimensional MP codes with two-code keying
articles.title_en: Two-Dimensional Polar Codes Improve Optical CDMA Performance
articles.excerpt_original: We propose what we believe to be a novel code family of two-dimensional multi-perfect polar codes (2-D MP codes) with two code keying (TCK) for spectral amplitude coding optical code division multiple access (SAC-OCDMA) networks. The proposed architecture using the transmitters in the optical line terminals (OLTs) efficiently generates code sequences using two mutually orthogonal states of polarization (SOPs) in the OCDMA system. At the receiver, the optical network unit (ONU) employs these code sequences to implement modified cross-correlation through two mutually orthogonal SOPs and TCK. The proposed system using 2-D MP codes with TCK achieves superior performance. Numerical results confirm that the 2-D MP codes with TCK achieve an exceptionally low bit error rate (BER) of 10 −22.67 , supporting data transmission rates up to 6.82 Gbps and demonstrating a received source power of −13.78dBm.

articles.title_original: MXene-enabled micro/nanofluidic transport interfaces: ordered nanochannels, hydration regulation, and responsive ion transport
articles.title_en: MXene Nanochannels Enable Responsive Ion-Transport Membranes
articles.excerpt_original: MXenes have emerged as promising building blocks for micro/nanofluidic transport interfaces because of their lamellar architecture, hydrophilic surface terminations, solution processability, and high electrical conductivity. Unlike conventional porous membranes, stacked MXene nanosheets can form slit-like nanochannels that confine water and ions within angstrom-to nanometer-scale spaces. Recent advances show that ion transport in MXene channels is governed not only by interlayer spacing, but also by channel alignment, lateral flake size, defect density, surface terminations, hydration structure, and interlayer chemistry. Ordered nanochannels, biomimetic sub-nanochannels, and directionally functionalized channel entrances have enabled improved ion selectivity and permeability. Meanwhile, confined water and cation intercalation can regulate local transport barriers, swelling behavior, and nanochannel stability. Crosslinked networks, hydrogel pillars, and mixed-dimensional assemblies further improve the mechanical reliability of MXene channels under aqueous conditions. In addition, light-responsive, pH-gated, voltage-gated, and electroconductive MXene membranes highlight the potential of dynamic ion transport and flow-responsive interfaces. This mini review summarizes recent progress in MXene-enabled micro/nanofluidic transport interfaces, emphasizing structure–transport–stability–response relationships and future opportunities for MEMS-compatible and device-oriented fluidic systems.
articles.summary_en: A mini-review examines MXene nanosheet membranes with ordered nanochannels for selective water and ion transport. It highlights hydration control, responsive gating, and structural strategies that improve permeability, stability, and device integration.

articles.title_original: Defect-Engineered Hexagonal Boron Nitride Enables Ionic Conduction for Lithium Metal Batteries
articles.title_en: Defect-Engineered h-BN Improves Lithium-Metal Battery Stability
articles.excerpt_original: The practical implementation of lithium metal anodes has been hindered by uncontrollable dendrite formation and interfacial instability. This study presents a defect engineering of multiplayer hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) that enhances ionic conductivity through argon ion irradiation. A cell-level demonstration was performed using commercially available, large-area CVD-grown h-BN films subjected to industrial-scale argon ion implantation. Direct evidence was provided by integration of these exfoliated flakes into a hybrid microfluidic-microelectronic chip, confirming that controlled vacancy defects transform h-BN into an efficient lithium-ion conductor while preserving its intrinsic electrical insulation. The results confirmed improved lithium-metal anode stability, achieving dendrite-free cycling with Li plating/stripping Coulombic efficiencies exceeding 99.5% for about 1000 cycles. Further assembly of irradiated h-BN in lithium-sulfur batteries effectively mitigates the polysulfide shuttle effect, sustaining over 97% specific capacity around 300 cycles. These results establish a robust, scalable interface engineering route for next-generation lithium metal batteries that combine high ionic transport with excellent electrical insulation.
articles.summary_en: Argon-ion irradiation introduced vacancy defects into CVD-grown hexagonal boron nitride, enabling ionic conduction while retaining electrical insulation. The treated material supported dendrite-free lithium cycling above 99.5% Coulombic efficiency for about 1,000 cycles and reduced polysulfide shuttling in lithium-sulfur cells.

articles.title_original: Three-dimensional hydrogel semiconductors for advanced bioelectronics

articles.excerpt_original: Abstract In this Research Highlights, we discuss a recently reported manufacturing strategy of dimensionally increased hydrogel OECT by engineering phase of double-network hydrogel and optimizing balanced electrical and ionic conductivity through porosity control. Owing to its tissue-like mechanical properties, with a Young’s modulus on the order of 10²–10³ kPa, this hydrogel semiconductor is particularly suitable for interfacing with complex three-dimensional biological tissues and is expected to mitigate inflammatory responses. Importantly, when incorporated into OECTs, the hydrogel channel maintained capacitance linearity even as the device dimensions were expanded, unlike conventional 2D film-based OECTs. Moreover, the transconductance (Gm) was substantially higher than that of stacked 2D film architectures, as the channel thickness increased. The highlighted work also demonstrated the potential of these OECTs for neuromorphic circuits that mimic biological neural networks. Future research directions would include a generalizable manufacturing strategy for 3D hydrogel OECTs that can accommodate semiconducting polymers beyond PEDOT:PSS and enable the development of not only p-type but also n-type devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report a porous double-network hydrogel semiconductor for three-dimensional organic electrochemical transistors (OECTs), combining tissue-like mechanics with balanced electrical and ionic conductivity. The devices retain capacitance linearity at larger dimensions, deliver higher transconductance than stacked 2D films, and show potential for neuromorphic bioelectronics.

articles.title_original: Synthesis and characterization of polycitric acid-functionalized MXene nanofluid for enhanced oil recovery
articles.title_en: Citric Acid-Functionalized MXene Nanofluid Improves Oil Recovery
articles.excerpt_original: In this study, a polycitric acid-functionalized MXene (Ti 3 C 2 T x ) (F-MX) nanofluid was synthesized, characterized, and evaluated for enhanced oil recovery (EOR). The F-MX nanofluid exhibited excellent colloidal stability in both deionized water and brines containing up to 5–20 wt% NaCl for 3 months. Interfacial tension (IFT) measurements demonstrated reductions from 45.7 ± 0.27 mN/m in deionized (DI) water and 48.3 ± 0.25 mN/m in brine to 34.99 ± 0.28 mN/m and 38.96 ± 0.32 mN/m, respectively, at a concentration of 0.1 wt%. Wettability tests revealed a reduction in contact angle from 155.06° ± 0.42 to 129.06° ± 0.29 at concentration of 0.1 wt%, indicating wettability modification. Adsorption experiments revealed that the adsorption capacity was higher in DI water than in saline conditions as increasing ionic strength reduces adsorption through electrostatic screening effects. Micromodel flooding experiments showed a substantial improvement in oil recovery, from 21% with conventional brine injection to 59% with F-MX nanofluid injection. articles.summary_en: Researchers synthesized a polycitric acid-functionalized MXene nanofluid with long-term stability in water and concentrated brines. In micromodel flooding tests, the formulation increased oil recovery from 21% with conventional brine to 59%, while reducing interfacial tension and modifying wettability.

articles.title_original: Frontiers in atomic-level manufacturing: atomic-scale friction
articles.title_en: Review maps atomic-scale friction for reliable MEMS/NEMS manufacturing
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract As micro/nanoelectromechanical systems (MEMS/NEMS) advance toward higher integration, device fabrication is entering the era of atomic and close-to-atomic scale manufacturing (ACSM). Interface friction has emerged as a critical factor affecting device performance and reliability. Atomic-scale friction is jointly determined by atomic structure, surface chemistry, and quantum effects, exhibiting behavior markedly different from macroscopic friction. This paper reviews recent advances in atomic-scale friction research, systematically summarizing major friction models and the influence of interatomic interactions, van der Waals forces, interfacial charge transfer, and energy dissipation mechanisms (phonon friction and electronic friction) on friction behavior. It also summarizes the primary physical mechanisms enabling ultra-low friction in two-dimensional (2D) materials, carbon materials, and semiconductor materials, while introducing relevant experimental methods, simulation techniques, and the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in friction research. This paper aims to provide a clear framework for understanding and controlling friction mechanisms at the atomic scale, offering theoretical and methodological references for designing highly reliable micro/nano devices and novel quantum devices.
articles.summary_en: The review examines how atomic structure, surface chemistry, quantum effects, and phonon/electronic dissipation govern friction in atomic-scale manufacturing. It highlights ultra-low-friction mechanisms in two-dimensional, carbon, and semiconductor materials, with implications for reliable micro/nano and quantum devices.

articles.title_original: Polarization‐Dependent Synaptic‐Like Electro‐Optical Response in Ferroelectric Nematic Liquid Crystals
articles.title_en: Semiconductor Interfaces Improve Synaptic-Like Liquid-Crystal Electro-Optics
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Ferroelectric nematic liquid crystals (FNLCs) exhibit spontaneous polarization and can be reoriented at low electric fields, enabling their use in electro‐optical applications. However, poor remanent polarization ( P r ) poses a significant barrier to the technology adoption of FNLCs. This study aims to overcome this hurdle by modifying the electrode–molecule interfaces of FNLCs with semiconductors to enhance P r . FNLCs with various semiconductor‐modified interfaces are characterized by polarization and current measurements, while optical responses are probed via second‐harmonic generation (SHG). Under a triangular‐shaped voltage, the semiconductor–FNLC–semiconductor (FNLC 1) configuration exhibits 1.5 times higher P r than a conventional FNLC system in the ferroelectric nematic (N F ) phase, reaching up to ∼4 µC cm − 2 at low‐switching fields (1.5–2.0 kV cm −1 ). Enhanced P r is also demonstrated with pulse programs, indicating slower relaxation of FNLC 1. This allows the system to retain the effect of previous stimulation, which is essential for emulating biological synapses through long‐ and short‐term electro‐optical responses. The cumulative current response from a single FNLC 1 unit to multiple units retains ∼90% after repeated cycles and enables optical texture modulation using the post‐current signal. Hence, the findings demonstrate the P r ‐enhancing effect of semiconductor interfaces, paving the way for low‐power synaptic‐like FNLCs.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report that semiconductor-modified interfaces increase remanent polarization in ferroelectric nematic liquid crystals by 1.5×, reaching approximately 4 µC cm⁻² at low switching fields. articles.title_original: Intrinsic Phonons as a Dynamic Control Knob for Catalytic Reactivity in 2D Materials
articles.title_en: Intrinsic Phonons Enable Dynamic Control of Catalytic Reactivity in 2D Materials
articles.excerpt_original: Catalytic activity is conventionally understood in terms of static electronic structure descriptors, with lattice vibrations treated as a passive background. Here we show that intrinsic phonon modes can serve as an active and selective control knob for catalytic reactivity in 2D materials. Using density functional theory, we demonstrate that mode-specific lattice excitations in transition metal dichalcogenides dynamically modulate their electronic structure, inducing direct-indirect bandgap transitions and substantial bandgap renormalization. In Janus WSSe, excitation of the A1 2 mode reduces the bandgap to 0.93 eV, significantly enhancing carrier transport. More importantly, these phonon-induced lattice distortions systematically tune adsorption energetics and reaction pathways. Using the oxygen evolution reaction as a model system, we find that phonon activation lowers the overpotential by up to 17%, arising from weakened adsorption of key intermediates. Crystal orbital Hamilton population and p-band center analyses reveal that this effect originates from phonon-driven modulation of orbital hybridization and bonding strength. Our results establish a dynamic, mode-selective paradigm for controlling catalytic processes via intrinsic lattice degrees of freedom, opening a route toward phonon-engineered electrocatalysis beyond static materials design.
articles.summary_en: Density-functional-theory calculations show that selectively exciting phonon modes in transition-metal dichalcogenides can alter bandgaps, adsorption energetics, and reaction pathways. In Janus WSSe, phonon activation reportedly reduces oxygen-evolution overpotential by up to 17%, suggesting a route to phonon-engineered electrocatalysis.

bulletin.title: Graphene Weekly Bulletin — Week ending 2026-08-02
bulletin.introduction: Research activity remains the principal driver, with graphene and graphene oxide functionalization recurring across separation media, protective and structural composites, thermal interfaces, and semiconductor photonics. The strongest technical pattern is application-specific materials engineering—controlling interfaces, porosity, coatings, and layer quality—rather than a single platform breakthrough. Commercial signals are concentrated in composites, additive-manufacturing feedstocks, and coated solar modules, while cable patents indicate adjacent infrastructure interest. However, most commercial announcements lack independently verified performance, volumes, or deployment evidence.

academic.blurb: A polyamine-assisted mechanochemical process simultaneously exfoliates and functionalizes graphene with polyethyleneimine. The resulting composite is reported to combine high CO₂ capacity and selectivity with humidity tolerance, cyclic stability and rapid electrothermal heating, making this a substantive industrial post-combustion capture candidate.

academic.blurb: SiO₂–graphene oxide and SiO₂–graphene oxide–activated carbon nanocomposites were fabricated with optimized porous structures and surface areas up to 127.03 m²/g. Their indicated capacity to address microplastics, heavy metals, dyes and other wastewater pollutants warrants attention, although removal performance is not quantified.

academic.blurb: CVD graphene photogating devices were demonstrated across mono-, bi- and trilayer material, with monolayer devices reaching 995 A/W sensitivity. The work directly addresses scalable graphene photodetection and usefully identifies layer number and contact fabrication as determinants of sensitivity and detectivity.

A waveguide-integrated twisted-bilayer graphene bolometer delivered 109 pW Hz−1/2 noise-equivalent power, 0.48 A/W responsivity and bandwidth above 67 GHz, receiving 120 Gbps signals. These device-level results provide concrete support for graphene integration in silicon photonics, communications and sensing.

Adding graphene nanopowder to glass-fiber/epoxy composites improved reported tensile strength, hardness and impact resistance. At 0.6 wt.% loading, the study reports respective gains of 256.25%, 49.4% and 60.83%, offering unusually specific evidence for lightweight structural-composite reinforcement.

academic.blurb: A low-temperature plasma-assisted process conformally grew vertically oriented graphene nanowalls on TiO₂, Al₂O₃ and SiO₂ nanotube scaffolds. The resulting hierarchical surfaces reportedly exceeded 170° contact angles without fluorine, presenting a potentially scalable route to omniphobic multifunctional coatings and interfaces.

academic.blurb: Graphene oxide/TiO₂ nanocomposites containing 3–11 wt% graphene oxide were made by simple mixing. Increasing oxide content reduced the reported TiO₂ optical band gap from 3.37 to 2.79 eV and shifted absorption toward visible light, supporting solar-energy relevance.

academic.blurb: In-situ work combines 532 nm pulsed-laser treatment with controlled electron-beam exposure to completely deoxygenate graphene oxide while preserving film integrity and restoring its sp² graphitic network. The localized process supports a credible route toward graphene synthesis, though scalability remains prospective.

A review examines graphene oxide synthesis, functionalization, reduction, characterization, and nanocomposite development, comparing established oxidation methods on scalability, safety, and environmental impact. It surveys applications in energy storage, water purification, catalysis, biosensing, flexible electronics, and biomedical systems while identifying challenges in reproducibility, sustainability, stability, and biosafety.

industry.blurb: HKUST researchers report a substrate-integrated thermal interface material combining laser-induced graphene with functionalized liquid-metal droplets. Compression forms a continuous metal pathway within the porous graphene network, targeting contact thermal resistance. The work is a specific graphene–metal composite advance, though it remains research-stage.

industry.blurb: A confined dual-catalyst CVD process reportedly produced adlayer-free monocrystalline graphene on Cu(111)/sapphire substrates. The team reports 20 six-inch wafers per batch and a four-order-of-magnitude reduction in adlayer-domain counts, offering unusually concrete pilot-scale evidence relevant to semiconductor-grade graphene manufacturing.

A capacitor-discharge process reportedly converts pre-carbonized water hyacinth into porous graphene-like carbon in about two seconds. Reported Cr(III) removal exceeds 95%, indicating potential relevance for water treatment, although the supplied account provides no independent validation or operating conditions.
